# **Script 8: "Why Does My Lower Back Keep Giving Out? (Ligament Damage and the Day It Takes From You)"**

Target length: 20 minutes (about 20 minutes total including the 1-minute pre-recorded mid-roll) \| Format: talking head, a lumbar spine model on the desk, on-screen clock graphic that changes with each section, on-screen text for the lists Framework notes are in brackets and are not spoken on camera.

Structure note: this script is built around one ordinary day, hour by hour, instead of a list of questions or "secrets." Each time of day teaches one idea. This is deliberately different from scripts 5 and 7\.

Before recording:

* \[INSERT REAL PATIENT\] marks the patient thread. The shape below is a placeholder. Swap in a real case and change identifying details.  
* \[VERIFY\] marks claims that need a source in hand before you say them.

Questions from your market that this script answers:

* "Why does my back go out when I bend over?"  
* "Why does my lower back feel like it's giving out?"  
* "Why is my sciatica not going away?"  
* "Can sciatica come back after it's gone?"  
* "Why do I keep getting the same pain back after it goes away?"  
* "Why did the doctor say there's nothing wrong when I'm clearly in pain?"

---

## **Video Description**

Take the free self-check assessment here: www\.thepostureacademy.com

Why does your lower back keep giving out? If you bend over to pick up a sock, reach into the back seat, or lift a laundry basket and your lower back suddenly catches, locks, or feels like it is about to give way, and it keeps happening even though your MRI and X-rays came back normal, this video explains one of the most overlooked causes: ligament damage that lets a joint in the lower spine move more than it should.

In this video, Dr. Spence, a chiropractic physician with 24 years of experience treating whiplash, car crash injuries, and ligament instability in the spine, walks through an ordinary day to show exactly where lumbar instability shows up: getting out of bed, sitting in the car, standing up after a long meeting, picking up a child, and lying down at night. You will learn why the pain can seem to come from nothing, why leg pain and sciatica-type symptoms can return after they fade, why a standard MRI can be normal, how a flexion and extension X-ray measures movement between the vertebrae, and what actually helps: stability work instead of aggressive stretching or cracking.

Topics covered in this video:

* Why does my lower back keep giving out when I bend over  
* Why does my back feel unstable or like it is going to give out  
* What is lumbar instability and what causes it  
* Can a past injury or car crash cause lasting low back instability  
* Why does sciatica or leg pain keep coming back after it goes away  
* Why was my lower back MRI normal when I still have pain  
* How is lower back instability diagnosed with flexion and extension X-rays  
* Why does stretching and cracking my back only help for a short time  
* What helps an unstable lower back besides surgery

Who this video is for: anyone with lower back pain that comes and goes, a back that catches or feels like it gives out with ordinary movements, or sciatica-type pain that keeps returning, especially after a car crash, a fall, a sports injury, or a lifting injury, and especially people who have been told their scans are normal.

This video is educational and is not a diagnosis. Loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness in the groin or inner thighs, progressive leg weakness, or severe pain after trauma needs emergency medical care.

\#LowerBackPain \#BackPain \#Sciatica \#LumbarInstability \#LigamentDamage \#BackGivesOut \#ChronicBackPain \#SpinalInstability \#CarCrashInjury \#ChiropracticCare \#ThePostureAcademy \#DrSpence

## **Thumbnail Suggestions**

Each thumbnail is matched to the headline with the same number, so the words on the thumbnail and the title agree.

1. (Headline 1\) A person bent halfway over to pick up a sock, one hand braced on the lower back, face tight with a "not again" expression. Text overlay: "BACK KEEPS GIVING OUT?"  
2. (Headline 2\) A simple diagram of two stacked vertebrae with a red arrow showing one sliding slightly forward past the other, and a rubber band stretched between them. Text overlay: "THE LIGAMENT IS LOOSE"  
3. (Headline 3\) A person sitting on the edge of a bed in the morning, hand on the lower back, looking at the floor. Text overlay: "NORMAL MRI. STILL HURTS."

## **Headline Suggestions**

1. Why Does My Lower Back Keep Giving Out?  
2. Lower Back Instability: The Ligament Problem Your MRI Can't See  
3. Normal MRI, Back Still Gives Out: Here's What's Going On

---

## **\[0:00-1:24\] COLD OPEN: The Sock**

\[ON CAMERA. Start mid-action, as if you're already telling it. Quiet, specific.\]

You bend over to pick up a sock.

Not a bowling ball. Not a bag of concrete. A sock.

And something in your lower back catches. Just for a second. A hot, sharp, wrong feeling, like a door that was closed a little too hard. You freeze. You wait to see how bad it's going to be.

Maybe it passes. Maybe it doesn't, and you spend the next three days walking like you're carrying something fragile.

And the part that makes you crazy is that you've done that exact movement ten thousand times.

I'm Dr. Spence. I'm a chiropractic physician and I've been treating spine injuries for 24 years. And the question I'm going to answer in this video is the one I hear in a hundred different forms. Why does my lower back keep giving out? And why, if something is really wrong, does nobody seem to be able to find it?

Here's the idea I'll build on. Your back isn't failing on the day it gives out. It's failing every day, a little, and that day is just when you notice.

To show you what I mean, I'm going to walk you through one ordinary day. Hour by hour. Pay attention to which parts sound like yours.

---

## **\[1:24-3:41\] 6:15 AM: GETTING OUT OF BED**

\[ON CAMERA. A clock graphic reads 6:15 AM. Slow, personal tone.\]

The alarm goes off. You roll toward the edge of the bed, and you do what a lot of people with this problem do. You negotiate.

You don't just sit up. You log-roll. You push with your arms. You pause on the edge of the mattress with your feet on the floor, and you take a breath before you stand.

If you do that, I want you to notice something. Nobody taught you that. Your body taught you that, because it learned that sitting up fast has a price.

Here is what's going on in that first minute. Overnight, your back muscles have been holding a quiet, low level of tension, because they've been guarding. Guarding is what muscles do when a joint underneath them can't be trusted. And as the night goes on, the tissues around that joint get stiff and a little swollen. So the first movements of the day are the stiffest, and you feel it right away.

Let me explain the structure underneath, because you can't understand the rest of this video without it.

\[Pick up the lumbar model.\]

Each vertebra in your lower back connects to the one above and the one below. Between them are the discs, the joints in the back called facets, and the ligaments. The ligaments are the tough bands that connect bone to bone, and they work as limit straps. Their job is to let a joint move through its normal range, and then say stop.

When those straps are healthy, the vertebrae glide through a small, controlled range. When one of those straps has been overstretched by a crash, a fall, a lifting injury, or years of repeated strain, it can become loose. And then the joint it was controlling can slide or tilt further than it should.

That's the thing I want you to understand for the rest of this video. When a joint can move too far, it doesn't always hurt all the time. It hurts when it goes past its limit. And that's why the pain seems to come and go for no reason.

---

## **\[3:41-5:11\] THE PATIENT THREAD**

\[INSERT REAL PATIENT. Shape only below. Use someone actual and change identifying details. Weave this in so it feels like a continuation of the morning scene.\]

\[ON CAMERA. Warmer, slower.\]

I want to introduce you to someone who lives this morning.

A man came to see me. Forty-eight. He owns a small landscaping company, so his back is also his livelihood. About six years earlier, he'd fallen off the back of a trailer. Landed flat. He was sore for a few weeks and went back to work.

Over the years the pattern changed. First it was a bad day here and there. Then it was a pattern of bad weeks. At the time he came to me, his back was "going out" about once a month. That's how he described it. Going out. He'd bend to tie a boot, or reach for a tool, and he'd be done for three or four days. Sometimes the pain went down his leg to the knee.

He'd had an MRI. It showed some mild wear that the radiologist called "age appropriate." He'd done physical therapy. He'd had injections once. He told me the thing that bothered him most wasn't the pain. It was that his son, who was in high school and worked for him in the summer, had started to look at him like he was fragile.

"I don't want my kid to see me as the guy who can't do it," he said.

\[Beat. Hold the pause.\]

Keep him in mind, because we're going to walk through his day too.

---

## **\[5:11-6:11\] MID-ROLL (self-sponsored, cuts in as a natural break, not announced as an ad)**

\[NATURAL BREAK. No spoken lead-in. The video cuts directly from the last line above into the pre-recorded segment below. This is intentional: no "here's our sponsor" framing, since this is your own segment, not a third-party ad.\]

\[\[ PRE-RECORDED SEGMENT: INSERTED IN EDITING. SCRIPT BELOW FOR REFERENCE \]\]

If pain came out of nowhere, or you got hurt in a crash, felt better for a while, and now it's crept back, you're not imagining it, and you're not the first person this has happened to.

I've sat across from hundreds of people telling me almost the exact same story. Scans came back clean. Doctors ran out of answers. And somehow, they walked away feeling like it was all in their head.

Here's the pattern I keep seeing. The pain isn't coming from nowhere. It's often ligament damage that never fully resolved, the kind that doesn't always show up on an X-ray or MRI.

I built a free self check to help you see if that's what's going on with you. It takes about 4 minutes, no catch.

If it turns something up, you're in good company, and there's likely a next step for you. The link's in the show notes. Alright, back to the video.

\[\[ END PRE-RECORDED SEGMENT \]\]

---

## **\[6:11-6:20\] RE-ENTRY**

\[ON CAMERA. Pick up mid-thought. Do not acknowledge a break took place.\]

So that's the morning. The stiffness, the log-roll, the negotiation. Let's keep going, because it gets more interesting once you're up and moving.

---

## **\[6:20-8:16\] 7:45 AM: THE DRIVE**

\[ON CAMERA. Clock graphic reads 7:45 AM.\]

You get in the car. Maybe thirty minutes of commuting. Maybe less.

By the time you pull into the parking lot, you notice a dull ache across the belt line. Or a deep pull at one side. And when you swing your legs out and stand up, there's that moment. A grab. A wince. You stand there next to your car for a second, waiting for it to let go.

Why does sitting do that?

When you sit, your lower spine settles into a curve that puts the ligaments at the back of the spine on a sustained stretch. \[VERIFY. Sitting loads the posterior ligamentous structures; have a source ready.\] A healthy ligament handles that without complaint. A ligament that's already lengthened and lax has less ability to resist. So the joint creeps. A tiny amount, for thirty minutes straight. Then you stand up quickly, and the joint has to snap back into position under load.

That grab you feel when you stand isn't random. That's the joint being asked to reposition itself, and the strap that should control it isn't doing its share.

This is also why a lot of people with this problem say, "I'm fine walking, I'm fine lying down, but sitting kills me." That pattern is a clue. When pain is worst at the transitions, from sitting to standing, from lying to sitting, from bending to upright, the joint is changing position under load. That's the situation where a loose ligament shows itself.

Now a quick fact check, because I don't want to scare you. This pattern is not proof of anything on its own. A stiff muscle and a loose ligament can look similar from the outside. But if this is you, it's a reason to ask the right question, not a reason to wait it out.

---

## **\[8:16-10:15\] 10:30 AM: THE MEETING**

\[ON CAMERA. Clock graphic reads 10:30 AM. A little lighter in tone.\]

You're in a long meeting. Or a long shift. Or you're holding a clipboard in a hallway for an hour.

Around the second hour, you start shifting. A little to the left. A little to the right. You cross your leg, then uncross it. You lean on one elbow.

People think you're restless. But what you're really doing is looking for the one position where the joint stops complaining.

This is the part where I want to talk about leg pain, because a lot of people watching have it. A burning line down the back of the thigh. A buzz in the calf. A heaviness in the foot. They've been told it's sciatica and they've been told it's a pinched nerve and then, three months later, it faded. And then, one day, it was back.

Here's how I see that. Sciatica is a name for a symptom. It's pain traveling along the sciatic nerve. It's not a diagnosis of the cause. The nerve roots exit your lower spine through small openings between the vertebrae. When a segment slides or tilts more than it should, even a small amount, that opening narrows and a nerve root can be irritated. The irritation can fade when you rest, because the joint settles. It can come back when you do something that asks the joint to move past its limit again.

That's the reason leg symptoms can disappear and reappear. Nothing healed in the meantime. The joint just went back inside its limit for a while.

\[Direct to camera.\]

If your leg pain has come back after it went away, tell me in the comments how many times. Once, twice, five times. I want to know what the real pattern looks like, because the answers are going to help a lot of people watching.

---

## **\[10:15-12:00\] 12:15 PM: THE TEST EVERYONE ASKS ABOUT**

\[ON CAMERA. Clock graphic reads 12:15 PM. Put a two-column list on screen: "What a standard scan answers" and "What it doesn't."\]

You're on your lunch break and you're scrolling, and you're asking the question I get asked more than any other. If something's wrong, why is my MRI normal?

Let me explain this clearly, because it's one of the biggest sources of confusion and, honestly, of self-doubt.

An MRI is a very good picture of discs, nerves, and swelling. It answers the question, is there a herniated disc, is a nerve being squeezed, is there a tumor or an infection. When it comes back normal or "age appropriate," that tells you those structures look okay.

What an MRI usually can't do is tell you how far a joint moves when you bend. You lie still in the machine. In that position, a loose joint can sit right where it belongs. So you get a clean picture of a spine that moves wrong.

The test that answers the movement question is a flexion and extension X-ray. You're X-rayed bending forward and then bending back. The clinician then measures how much each vertebra translates, or slides, and how much it tilts compared with the ones above and below. Those measurements can be compared with established thresholds for instability. It's an objective measurement of how the spine moves, and that's different from a picture of how it looks at rest. A standard medical reference on segmental instability lists this kind of bending X-ray as part of how the problem is evaluated.

So when somebody tells you, "Your scans look fine," here's a better answer to give them. "Fine at rest. Has anybody measured how it moves?"

---

## **\[12:00-13:42\] 3:30 PM: THE PICKUP LINE**

\[ON CAMERA. Clock graphic reads 3:30 PM. Slower, emotional.\]

It's the afternoon. Maybe you have a child. Maybe a grandchild. Maybe a niece who runs at you like a cannonball. Maybe nothing like that, and the moment is a different one: a heavy box, a bag of groceries, a dog that needs to be lifted into the truck.

You see it coming and your body runs the math before you know it's running.

Can I lift that? What happens if I bend that way? Do I have time to set up my feet first? Will I pay for it tomorrow?

This is the cost that nobody puts on a chart. It's not the pain. It's the constant calculation.

Our landscaper told me he'd started saying, "Let me get that," and then letting his son take the heavy end. He told himself it was teaching the kid. In his heart, he knew it wasn't. He'd started delegating his own life.

I hear versions of this every week. A mother who can't carry her toddler up the stairs without bracing. A grandfather who stopped getting down on the floor to play. A woman who stopped gardening, which she loved, because she couldn't be sure she'd get back up.

\[Direct to camera.\]

Here's something that I want you to understand for the rest of this video. When you start protecting your life around a body part, that is not weakness. That's information. Your body is telling you a joint can't be trusted yet. The goal isn't to ignore it. The goal is to fix the reason it can't be trusted.

---

## **\[13:42-15:18\] 5:30 PM: THE STRETCH AND THE CRACK**

\[ON CAMERA. Clock graphic reads 5:30 PM. More direct, slightly firmer.\]

You get home. You're sore. And you do what almost everyone does with a sore back. You stretch it.

You pull a knee to your chest. You fold forward over your legs. You twist side to side. Maybe you lie on the floor and have someone press on you until something pops.

And it feels great for a few minutes. Honestly, it does.

Then an hour later, or the next morning, you're tighter than before.

I have to be really clear here, because this is the most useful thing in this video if you take it seriously. If the underlying problem is a joint that moves too far, then forcing it through more range, or cracking it hard, is the opposite of what it needs.

The relief you feel after a hard crack is real. The muscles guarding the joint let go for a moment. But the ligament that was already lax just got stretched a little more. So the muscles have to clamp down harder next time to compensate. And you're locked in a cycle where you need more and more to get the same few hours of relief.

That's the "my chiropractor stopped helping" story. It's the "my physical therapist's stretches stopped working" story. It isn't that those people did something wrong. It's that a loose joint needs a different approach.

This is why, for this pattern, I don't treat flexibility as the goal. The goal is stability.

---

## **\[15:18-17:13\] 7:00 PM: WHAT STABILITY ACTUALLY MEANS**

\[ON CAMERA. Clock graphic reads 7:00 PM. Calm, explanatory. Use the model.\]

Let me explain what I mean by that word, because it sounds vague and it isn't.

Along your spine there are small muscles that attach from one vertebra to the next. They're not the big muscles you see in the mirror. They're deep, short, and very specific. Their job isn't to move you. Their job is to hold each segment steady while you move.

When the ligaments are healthy, those small muscles barely have to work. The ligaments carry most of the load. When the ligaments are loose, those little muscles have to take over a job they weren't built for. And what usually happens is that they get tired and stop firing well, or they fire late.

The point of stability work is to retrain those small muscles to turn on in time and hold the segment where it belongs. Gently, in small doses your back can tolerate, and in a progression. Not heavy lifting. Not aggressive stretching. Precise, controlled work.

Three principles for it. First, you work inside your safe range, not at the end of it. Second, you build endurance before you build strength, because those deep muscles need to hold for a long time, not lift a lot at once. And third, you progress slowly, because the whole point is to widen the margin your back can handle without crossing the line.

What do people notice? The first thing usually isn't that the pain disappears. It's that the flare-ups get farther apart. Then shorter. Then the back stops "going out" over small things. That's the signal.

It takes weeks to months. Not days. Every back is different, so I won't hand you a date. What I'll give you is the signal to watch for.

---

## **\[17:13-18:32\] 9:30 PM: WHAT TO DO ON A BAD DAY**

\[ON CAMERA. Clock graphic reads 9:30 PM. Practical, steady.\]

Now, you might be in a flare right now. So here's what I'd do.

Don't take to the bed for days. Complete rest makes a stiff, guarded back worse. Short walks, on flat ground, at an easy pace.

Change position often. Don't hold any one posture for more than a short stretch. Stand up, walk to the kitchen, sit back down.

Use heat if it feels good. It helps guarded muscles let go.

Skip hard stretching and skip hard cracking. Let the muscles settle.

When you bend, bend from the hips, and keep one hand on a surface when you can. When you lift, bring the load close, and don't twist while you carry it.

Keep a short log. What set it off? A long drive. A heavy bag. A bad night's sleep. After a month, you'll see your pattern, and the pattern tells you what your margin looks like.

And know your red flags. Loss of control of your bladder or bowels, numbness in the groin or inner thighs, leg weakness that's getting worse, or severe pain after a fall or a crash. Those aren't a "try this at home." Those are an emergency room.

---

## **\[18:32-20:05\] 11:00 PM: LYING DOWN**

\[ON CAMERA. Clock graphic reads 11:00 PM. Quiet. Slow.\]

It's the end of the day. You lie down, and for a lot of you, this is the best part, because this is the position where the joint is unloaded and the muscles can finally relax.

Then you turn over in the middle of the night and you wake up.

Here's what I want to say to the person lying in the dark, running the math for tomorrow.

You are not fragile. You are not lazy. You are not making it up. You may very well have a joint that was injured once and never fully got its stability back, and nobody ever measured it. And the thing that makes it hard isn't that it's unfixable. It's that it's invisible to the tests you've been given.

Our landscaper, by the way. He got the bending X-ray. One segment in the lower back was moving more than the ones around it, and it lined up with the fall off the trailer. We started with stability work, slowly. About two months in, he told me the thing he noticed first wasn't less pain. It was that he'd bent over to tie his boot, felt that old catch begin, and it didn't finish. It stopped. He said he stood there for a second, almost waiting for it.

And then, he told me, he picked up the heavy end of the beam, and his son just watched.

---

## **\[20:05-20:39\] THE OFFER**

\[ON CAMERA, warmer tone, slower pace.\]

If you've been living with a back that gives out, or leg pain that keeps coming back, and the tests have all said normal, that pattern is exactly what The Posture Academy was built around.

It's a structured program for the joints that ligament damage leaves unsupported. A progressive plan that builds stability first and strength after, so your back has a bigger margin and the flare-ups get farther apart and shorter.

There's a link below this video if you'd like guided help with that.

---

## **\[20:39-21:18\] WHO THIS IS FOR, AND WHO IT ISN'T**

\[ON CAMERA. This section sits between the offer and the fixed CTA on purpose. Do not move it.\]

I want to be honest about who this is for.

If you threw your back out once, it healed completely, and it hasn't come back, this probably isn't about you, and I'm glad.

This is for the person whose back keeps going out over small things. The one who's learned to log-roll out of bed. The one who has a leg that burns, fades, and returns. The one who has been told the scans are normal and has started to wonder if the problem is in their head.

It isn't. Nobody has measured how your back moves yet.

---

## **\[21:18-21:38\] SOFT CTA: SELF-CHECK ASSESSMENT (FIXED, USE VERBATIM IN EVERY VIDEO)**

\[ON CAMERA, warm, low-pressure tone. This section is identical in every video.\]

There's one thing I want you to do right now. Click the link in the description below and take the free self-check assessment. It takes about four minutes, and it'll give you a clearer picture of what's actually going on with your neck or back. No catch, just answers.

---

## **\[21:38-21:57\] CLOSE**

\[ON CAMERA, calm, direct eye contact. Different from the other videos on purpose.\]

Tell me in the comments what your "sock" is. The small, ordinary thing that your back takes a swing at. I read every one.

If this sounded like your day, subscribe. There's more on this coming, and you're not the only one running that math.

I'm Dr. Spence.

\[END\]

# **Script 9: "Why Do I Get Headaches at the Base of My Skull? (When Your Headache Starts in Your Neck)"**

Target length: 20 minutes (about 20 minutes total including the 1-minute pre-recorded mid-roll) \| Format: talking head, a cervical spine model with the skull base on the desk, a small notebook as a prop (the "headache log"), on-screen text for the lists. Framework notes are in brackets and are not spoken on camera.

Structure note: this script follows the Hook, Story, 3 Secrets, Offer format. It is built around one patient's headache log. Each secret is tied to a page in the log. This is deliberately different from Script 8, which walked through one day hour by hour.

Before recording:

* \[INSERT REAL PATIENT\] marks the patient thread. The shape below is a placeholder. Swap in a real case and change identifying details.  
* \[VERIFY\] marks claims that need a source in hand before you say them.

Questions from your market that this script answers:

* "Why do I get headaches at the base of my skull?"  
* "Can neck problems cause headaches?"  
* "Why do I have a headache every day since my car accident?"  
* "Why does my headache start in my neck and go behind my eye?"  
* "Is it a migraine or is it coming from my neck?"  
* "Why did my CT scan come back normal when I still have headaches?"

---

## **Video Description**

Take the free self-check assessment here: [www\.thepostureacademy.com](http://www.thepostureacademy.com)

Why do you get headaches at the base of your skull? If your headache starts in the back of your head or the top of your neck, then spreads over the top to your forehead or behind one eye, and it keeps coming back even though your CT scan or MRI was normal, this video explains one of the most overlooked causes: a headache that starts in the neck, often after ligament damage in the top two joints of the spine.

In this video, Dr. Spence, a chiropractic physician with 24 years of experience treating whiplash, car crash injuries, and ligament instability in the spine, walks through one patient's headache log to show how a neck headache works. You will learn how the nerves of the upper neck share a relay station with the nerves of the face and forehead, the clues that point to a neck source instead of a migraine, why the top two joints of the neck depend on ligaments more than any other joints in the spine, why massage and cracking only help for a few hours, how motion X-rays measure what a standard scan misses, and what actually helps: deep neck stability work.

Topics covered in this video:

* Why do I get headaches at the base of my skull  
* Can a neck problem cause headaches behind the eye or in the forehead  
* What is a cervicogenic headache  
* How to tell a neck headache from a migraine  
* Can a car crash or whiplash cause headaches that last for years  
* Why was my CT or MRI normal when I still have headaches  
* Why does massage or cracking my neck only help for a short time  
* What helps a headache that starts in the neck

Who this video is for: anyone with headaches that start at the back of the head or top of the neck, headaches that come with neck pain or a stiff neck, or headaches that started after a car crash, a fall, or a sports injury, especially people who have been told their scans are normal and their headaches are "just stress."

This video is educational and is not a diagnosis. A sudden, severe headache that feels like the worst of your life, a headache with fever and a stiff neck, a headache with confusion, weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or vision loss, or a severe headache after a blow to the head needs emergency medical care.

\#Headache \#NeckPain \#CervicogenicHeadache \#HeadacheRelief \#Whiplash \#LigamentDamage \#NeckHeadache \#ChronicHeadache \#CarCrashInjury \#ChiropracticCare \#ThePostureAcademy \#DrSpence

## **Thumbnail Suggestions**

Each thumbnail is matched to the headline with the same number, so the words on the thumbnail and the title agree.

1. (Headline 1\) A person with the fingertips of one hand pressed into the base of the skull, eyes closed, face tight. Text overlay: "HEADACHE STARTS HERE?"  
2. (Headline 2\) A simple side-view diagram of the head and neck with a red line running from the top of the neck, over the head, to behind one eye. Text overlay: "IT'S YOUR NECK"  
3. (Headline 3\) A person holding a printed scan report in one hand, the other hand on the back of the head. Text overlay: "NORMAL SCAN. DAILY HEADACHES."

## **Headline Suggestions**

1. Why Do I Get Headaches at the Base of My Skull?  
2. Neck Headaches: When Your Headache Is Coming From Your Neck  
3. Normal Scan, Headaches Every Day: Check Your Neck

---

## **\[0:00-1:20\] HOOK: The Hand on the Back of the Head**

\[ON CAMERA. Start quiet. Reach back and press your fingertips into the base of your own skull as you say the first line.\]

I can usually tell what kind of headache someone has before they say a word.

They walk in, sit down, and when I ask where it hurts, they don't point to their forehead. They reach back and press their fingers right here. Into the base of the skull. Right where the head sits on the neck.

Then they drag their hand up and over the top of the head, and they stop at one eye.

"It starts here," they say. "And it ends up here."

If you just did that with your own hand, this video is for you.

I'm Dr. Spence. I'm a chiropractic physician and I've been treating spine injuries for 24 years. And the question I'm going to answer in this video is one I hear every single week. Why do I get headaches at the base of my skull? And why do they keep coming back when every test says I'm fine?

Here's the short answer, and I'll spend the rest of the video proving it to you. A lot of headaches that feel like they live in your head are actually starting in your neck. Your head is just where you feel them.

---

## **\[1:20-3:45\] THE STORY: The Headache Log**

\[INSERT REAL PATIENT. Shape only below. Use someone actual and change identifying details.\]

## **\[4:55-8:00\] SECRET 1: YOUR NECK CAN SEND PAIN TO YOUR FACE**

\[ON CAMERA. On-screen text: "Secret 1: Your neck and your face share a switchboard." Pick up the spine model.\]

Every single headache in her log started in the same place. The base of the skull on the right. And almost every one ended up behind her right eye.

Now, if you're thinking, "My eye is nowhere near my neck. How can my neck cause pain behind my eye?" that's a great question. Here's how.

\[Point to the top of the neck on the model.\]

The nerves that come out of the top three joints of your neck carry signals from the muscles, joints, and ligaments up here at the base of the skull. Those signals travel into a relay station at the bottom of the brain.

Here's the important part. That same relay station also takes signals from the nerve that covers your forehead, your temple, and the area around your eye. \[VERIFY. The upper cervical nerves and the trigeminal nerve converge in the trigeminocervical nucleus; have a source ready.\]

Think of it like an old telephone switchboard where two lines got wired into the same plug. When a call comes in, the operator can't always tell which line it came from.

So when a joint or ligament at the top of your neck is irritated and sends a pain signal, your brain can read it as pain behind your eye. Or in your forehead. Or in your temple. The problem is in your neck. The pain shows up in your head.

There's a name for this. A cervicogenic headache. "Cervico" means neck. "Genic" means starting from. A headache that starts in the neck. It's a recognized diagnosis in the international classification that headache doctors use. \[VERIFY. ICHD-3 code 11.2.1, cervicogenic headache.\]

And this is where a lot of people get stuck. If you treat that headache like it's coming from the head, with headache medicine, dark rooms, and stress advice, you may take the edge off. But you never touch the place where it starts.

\[Direct to camera.\]

Quick question for you. Where does your headache start? Not where it ends up. Where it starts. Put it in the comments. Base of the skull, temples, forehead, behind the eye. I want to see the pattern.

## **\[8:00-11:45\] SECRET 2: WHERE IT STARTS TELLS YOU WHERE IT LIVES**

\[ON CAMERA. On-screen text: "Secret 2: The clues are in the pattern." Open the notebook. Bring up the list on screen one line at a time as you say each clue.\]

The second thing I found in her log was the pattern. And the pattern is your best clue, because a neck headache behaves differently from other headaches.

I'm going to give you five clues. None of them prove anything on their own. But if you check off three or four, it's worth asking whether your neck is involved.

Clue number one. It's one-sided, and it's usually the same side. Her headaches were on the right almost every time. They didn't switch sides from one headache to the next.

Clue number two. It starts in the back and travels forward. Base of the skull first, then over the top, then the forehead or behind the eye. Not the other way around.

Clue number three. Your neck sets it off. Her log was full of entries like "grading papers at the kitchen table," "long drive to my sister's," "slept on the couch." Looking down for a long time. Holding your head still in one position. Sleeping with your neck bent. If certain neck positions start the headache, that's a big clue.

Clue number four. Your neck doesn't turn as far as it used to. When I checked her, she could turn her head to the left just fine. To the right, she stopped short, and it pulled at the base of her skull. Many people with this problem don't notice how much they've lost until someone measures it. They just turn their shoulders instead.

Clue number five. Pressing at the base of the skull reproduces it. When I pressed on the upper joints of her neck on the right side, she said, "That's it. That's my headache." That's a very telling moment.

\[Close the notebook.\]

Now, how is that different from a migraine? I want to be careful here, because migraines are real and they're common, and some people have both. A classic migraine often switches sides, often comes with nausea and a strong sensitivity to light and sound, and often isn't set off by neck position. \[VERIFY. Have migraine vs cervicogenic headache feature comparison source ready.\] A neck headache tends to stay on one side, start in the neck, and come with a stiff, limited neck.

So the point isn't to diagnose yourself from a YouTube video. The point is to walk into your next appointment and say, "My headache starts in my neck, it's always on the same side, and looking down sets it off. Has anyone checked my neck?"

That one sentence changes the conversation.

## **\[11:45-15:30\] SECRET 3: THE TOP OF YOUR NECK IS HELD TOGETHER BY LIGAMENTS**

\[ON CAMERA. On-screen text: "Secret 3: The top two joints run on ligaments." Pick up the spine model and point to the skull and the top two vertebrae.\]

The third thing in her log was the date the headaches started. About a month after the crash. And that brings us to the part almost nobody explains.

The top two joints of your neck are different from every other joint in your spine.

Down here in the rest of your neck, the bones stack on each other with discs in between, and the shape of the bones helps keep them in line.

Up here, it's different. The top bone in your neck is basically a ring. The second bone has a small peg that sticks up through that ring. That's the joint that lets you turn your head left and right. It's built for motion. Lots of motion. \[VERIFY. Roughly half of neck rotation happens at C1-C2; have a source ready.\]

And because it's built for motion, the bones don't hold it together very well on their own. What holds it together are ligaments. Strong bands that hold the peg against the ring and connect the top of the neck to the base of the skull.

Here's what happens in a crash. Even a slow one. Your body is held by the seat belt, but your head keeps going. The head whips forward and back faster than your muscles can react. The ligaments at the top of the neck can be stretched past their limit. Not torn in half. Stretched. Overstretched ligaments can heal looser than they were. \[VERIFY. Have a source on upper cervical ligament injury in whiplash.\]

And when the top joints move a little more than they should, the small muscles at the base of your skull try to do the ligaments' job. They clamp down. All day. Every day. They get tight, tired, and sore. That irritation feeds right into that switchboard I told you about.

That's the headache.

This also explains something that probably drives you crazy. Why does a massage feel amazing, and then the headache is back by the next day? Why does cracking your neck help for an hour, then not at all?

Because the massage relaxes the muscles that are guarding. For a little while. But the muscles were guarding for a reason. The joint underneath isn't stable. So they tighten right back up.

And cracking? I'll be blunt. Taking a joint at the top of the neck that's already moving too much, and forcing it hard and fast through even more motion, makes no sense to me. That's the last thing a loose joint needs. It's like fixing a wobbly table leg by kicking it.

Now, the question I always get. If this is real, why didn't my scan show it?

A CT scan or MRI of your head looks at your brain. It's looking for bleeding, a tumor, a stroke. It's a very important test, and if yours was normal, that's good news. But it isn't looking at how the top of your neck moves.

Even a standard neck X-ray or MRI is taken while you hold still. A joint that moves too far when you turn or bend can sit right where it belongs when you're still. So the picture looks normal.

The way to see how the neck moves is to take X-rays while it moves. Bending forward and bending back. Then the clinician measures how much each bone slides and tilts compared with the ones around it. \[VERIFY. Have a source on flexion and extension radiographs for cervical instability.\] That's a measurement of motion, not a picture at rest.

So when she told me her CT was normal, I said, "Good. Your brain is fine. Now let's look at your neck."

## **\[15:30-17:30\] WHAT HELPS**

\[ON CAMERA. Calm, practical. On-screen text for each point.\]

So what actually helps a headache that starts in the neck?

The goal is the same as with any loose joint. Not more flexibility. More stability.

There are small, deep muscles on the front of your neck that hold your head steady on top of your spine. In people with neck headaches, those muscles often don't hold well. They tire out fast. So the big muscles in the back of the neck take over, and they tighten up. \[VERIFY. Have a source on deep neck flexor endurance in neck pain and headache.\]

Training those deep muscles to hold, gently, for longer and longer, is one of the most studied approaches for this kind of headache. \[VERIFY. Jull et al. 2002 randomized trial of exercise and manipulative therapy for cervicogenic headache; have the citation ready.\] It isn't heavy. It isn't dramatic. A small nod of the head, held, and repeated. Built up slowly over weeks.

A few other things that help while you work on that.

Raise your screen. If you look down at a laptop or a phone for hours, bring it up to eye level. Every hour your head is tipped forward, those muscles at the base of your skull are working overtime.

Take breaks from holding still. Set a timer. Every thirty minutes, look up, turn your head gently both ways, and reset.

Check your pillow. You want your neck level with the rest of your spine when you sleep, not bent up or dropped down.

Skip the hard cracking. Let the guarding muscles settle on their own.

And keep a log. Just like she did. Where it started, what you were doing, what time. After a month, your pattern will be on the page.

And know your red flags. A sudden headache that feels like the worst of your life. A headache with fever and a stiff neck. Headache with confusion, weakness, numbness, trouble talking, or losing vision. A severe headache after a hit to the head. Those are not a "watch a video and try this." Those are an emergency room.
